idiom_name: wrapper class implementing the interface + hand-written forwarders (the JDK's FilterInputStream pattern)
implementation_notes: Java's canonical realization is the one the JDK itself uses: `FilterInputStream` 'simply overrides all methods of InputStream with versions that pass all requests to the contained input stream', and subclasses override only what they change. The delegate is a final field injected through the constructor and each forwarder is one line; the alternative for wide interfaces is `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`, which lets the JVM generate the implementing class and route every interface call to an `InvocationHandler`. Written forwarding stays the right default because it is compile-time checked, keeps the wrapper's surface deliberate and costs no reflection - reach for the proxy machinery when the interface is large, the wrapper must intercept generically, or the delegate is chosen at run time.
pitfalls: Forwarders are maintained by hand: a method added to the interface breaks the wrapper only when it is recompiled against the new interface (otherwise an AbstractMethodError surfaces at run time), and a method added to the delegate's concrete class is invisible to the wrapper by construction.

`equals`/`hashCode`/`toString` are not delegated by a plain wrapper - the wrapper keeps its own identity, so it is equal to nothing the delegate equals; decide whether to forward them or to document identity semantics.
Each forwarded call is still one extra virtual dispatch, and holding the delegate as a concrete class instead of the interface removes the substitutability the wrapper was built for.

variants.name: Dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy)
variants.idiom_name: Proxy.newProxyInstance(...) + InvocationHandler forwarding to a delegate
variants.implementation_notes: `Proxy.newProxyInstance` creates a class at run time that implements the named interfaces and encodes every call as `(proxy, method, args)` to a single handler, which typically forwards with `method.invoke(delegate, args)`; this removes the boilerplate for wide interfaces and is the mechanism behind Spring AOP and most mocking frameworks. It is interface-only (a class's other methods, fields and non-public members are unreachable), the order of the interface list is significant when they repeat a signature, and `hashCode`/`equals`/`toString` are dispatched to the handler as well, so the handler must decide how to answer them. Use it when interception is generic; keep the written wrapper when the surface should be narrow and deliberate.
variants.code_sketch:
Store delegate = new FileStore();
Store proxy = (Store) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
        Store.class.getClassLoader(),
        new Class<?>[] { Store.class },
        (p, method, args) -> method.invoke(delegate, args));  // no wrapper class written
pitfalls: Interface-only: you cannot proxy a class or reach fields and non-interface members of the target, so the delegate must be exposed through an interface.

`InvocationTargetException` wraps every business exception, and Object's methods (equals/hashCode/toString) are dispatched to the handler, so their semantics become handler-dependent unless special-cased.
Reflection on every call makes this the slowest realization, and the declaring class of the Method passed to the handler can change when the order of proxy interfaces changes.
